t.1.1.1: The ascetic Vālmīki questioned Nārada, the foremost among sages, who was ever devoted to austerity and the study of the Veda, and who was the best of those skilled in speech.
t.1.1.2: Who indeed in this world at present is virtuous, and who is valorous, knowing dharma and grateful, truthful in speech and firm in his vows?
t.1.1.3: Who is endowed with good conduct, and who is devoted to the welfare of all beings? Who is learned, who is capable, and who alone is pleasing to behold?
t.1.1.5: I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is great. O great sage, you are able to know such a man.
t.1.1.4: Who is self-possessed, who has conquered anger, who is wise and free from envy? Whom do even the gods fear when his wrath is roused in battle?
t.1.1.6: Having heard these words of Vālmīki, Nārada, knower of the three worlds, addressed him with "Listen!" and, delighted, spoke these words.
t.1.1.7: O sage, the qualities you have named are many and hard to find together. Having considered them, I shall tell you; let the man endowed with them be heard of.
t.1.1.8: Born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku, there is one known among the people by the name of Rāma. He is self-controlled, of great valour, radiant, steadfast, and master of his senses.
t.1.1.9: He is wise, skilled in statecraft, eloquent, glorious, and a destroyer of his foes; broad-shouldered and mighty-armed, he has a neck shaped like a conch shell and a strong jaw.
t.1.1.10: He is broad-chested, a mighty archer, with collarbones deep-set in flesh, a subduer of foes; his arms reach down to his knees, his head is well-formed, his forehead fine, and his stride full of valor.
t.1.1.11: He is well-proportioned, with limbs evenly and symmetrically formed, of glossy complexion, and full of splendour; broad-chested and large-eyed, he is graced with fortune and bears auspicious marks.
t.1.1.12: He knows what is right, is true to his word, and is devoted to the welfare of his subjects; he is renowned, endowed with knowledge, pure, self-controlled, and steadfast in concentration.
t.1.1.13: He is the protector of the world of living beings and the guardian of dharma; he knows the true essence of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, and he is firmly grounded in the science of archery.
t.1.1.14: He knows the true meaning of all the śāstras, is possessed of a strong memory and ready wit, is beloved of all the worlds, virtuous, of undaunted spirit, and discerning.
t.1.1.15: Like the ocean by the rivers, he is ever approached by the good; noble, equal toward all, he is always singularly pleasing to behold.
t.1.1.16: And he, endowed with every virtue, the increaser of Kausalyā's joy, is like the ocean in depth and like the Himavān in steadfastness.
t.1.1.17: He is like Viṣṇu in valor and as pleasing to behold as the moon; in anger he is like the fire of universal destruction, and in forbearance he is equal to the earth.
t.1.1.19: Out of affection, King Daśaratha, lord of the earth, wished to install as crown prince his beloved eldest son, who was endowed with the most excellent virtues.
t.1.1.18: In generosity he is equal to Dhanada, and in truthfulness he is like a second Dharma. Him, Rāma, thus endowed with such virtues and whose valor is true…
t.1.1.20: Then, seeing the preparations for his consecration, the queen Kaikayī, his wife, who had long ago been granted a boon, asked for this boon: the banishment of Rāma and the consecration of Bharata.
t.1.1.21: Bound by the noose of dharma because of his promised word, King Daśaratha banished Rāma, his beloved son.
t.1.1.22: That hero went to the forest, faithfully keeping his promise, at the direction of his father's word and for the sake of pleasing Kaikeyī.
t.1.1.23: As he went, his dear brother Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with humility and the increaser of Sumitrā's joy, followed him out of affection.
t.1.1.24: Sītā too, his bride, the best of women, endowed with every auspicious mark, followed Rāma, as Rohiṇī follows the moon.
t.1.1.25: Followed a long way by the townspeople and by his father Daśaratha, he dismissed the charioteer at Śṛṅgaverapura, on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
t.1.1.27: Having made a pleasant dwelling, the three of them, delighting in the forest and resembling gods and gandharvas, lived there happily.
t.1.1.26: Going from forest to forest and crossing rivers with abundant water, they reached Citrakūṭa at the command of Bharadvāja.
t.1.1.28: When Rāma had gone to Citrakūṭa, King Daśaratha, stricken with grief for his son, went to heaven, lamenting his son.
t.1.1.29: But when he had died, Bharata, though urged to take the kingship by the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha, did not desire the kingdom, mighty as he was; that hero went to the forest to win the favour of Rāma's feet.
t.1.1.30: And having given him his sandals as a pledge for the kingdom, Bharata's elder brother then, again and again, urged Bharata to turn back.
t.1.1.31: He, not having obtained his wish at all, touched Rāma's feet and ruled the kingdom from Nandigrāma, longing for Rāma's return.
t.1.1.32: But Rāma, perceiving that the people of the city would come there again, entered the Daṇḍaka forests with a single-minded resolve.
t.1.1.33: Having slain the rākṣasa Virādha, he saw Śarabhaṅga, and also Sutīkṣṇa and Agastya, and likewise Agastya's brother.
t.1.1.34: And at the word of Agastya, greatly delighted, he accepted the bow of Indra, a sword, and two quivers whose arrows never run out.
t.1.1.35: While Rāma was dwelling in the forest together with the forest-dwellers, all the sages came to him for the slaying of the Asuras and Rākṣasas.
t.1.1.36: While he was dwelling right there, Śūrpaṇakhā, a rākṣasī who could take any form at will and who lived in Janasthāna, was disfigured by him.
t.1.1.37: Then all the rākṣasas who had risen up for battle at the words of Śūrpaṇakhā, and Khara, and Triśiras, and the rākṣasa Dūṣaṇa as well…
t.1.1.38: In battle Rāma slew their followers as well; fourteen thousand of the Rākṣasas were slain.
t.1.1.39: Then, having heard of the slaughter of his kinsmen, Rāvaṇa, stupefied with rage, chose as his helper a rākṣasa named Mārīca.
t.1.1.40: Rāvaṇa was dissuaded again and again by Mārīca: 'O Rāvaṇa, a conflict with one so mighty is not fitting for you.'
t.1.1.41: But disregarding those words, Rāvaṇa, driven on by Time, then went together with Mārīca to his hermitage.
t.1.1.43: Seeing the vulture slain and hearing that Maithilī had been carried off, Rāghava, burning with grief, his senses overwhelmed, lamented.
t.1.1.42: Having the two princes lured far away by that master of illusion, he carried off Rāma's wife, after slaying the vulture Jaṭāyus.
t.1.1.44: Then, stricken with that very grief, having cremated the vulture Jaṭāyus, and searching for Sītā in the forest, he caught sight of a rākṣasa.
t.1.1.45: The mighty-armed one slew the demon named Kabandha, deformed in shape and dreadful to behold, and burned him, and he went to heaven.
t.1.1.46: And he told him, "O Rāghava, go to Śabarī, the female ascetic who practices dharma and is skilled in dharma." Then that greatly splendorous destroyer of enemies went to Śabarī.
t.1.1.47: Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, duly honored by Śabarī, met with the monkey Hanumān on the bank of the Pampā.
t.1.1.48: And at the word of Hanumān, mighty Rāma met with Sugrīva and told Sugrīva all that had happened.
t.1.1.49: Then the king of the monkeys, grieving, out of affection told Rāma everything concerning the account of his enmity, and there the monkey also described the strength of Vālin.
t.1.1.51: But Rāghava, to give him proof, flung the mighty carcass of Dundubhi with his big toe a full ten yojanas.
t.1.1.50: Then Rāma promised the slaying of Vālin, yet Sugrīva remained ever doubtful about Rāghava's prowess.
t.1.1.52: And then, with a single great arrow, he pierced the seven sāla trees, the mountain, and even Rasātala, thereby creating confidence at that time.
t.1.1.53: Then, glad at heart and reassured by him, that great monkey went together with Rāma to Kiṣkindhā, to its cave.
t.1.1.54: Then Sugrīva, the best of monkeys, golden-tawny in hue, roared; at that mighty roar the lord of the monkeys came forth.
t.1.1.56: And he, the bull among monkeys, having gathered all the monkeys together, sent them forth in every direction, eager to find the daughter of Janaka.
t.1.1.55: Then, at Sugrīva's word, Rāghava slew Vālin in battle and installed Sugrīva himself in that kingdom.
t.1.1.57: Then, at the word of the vulture Sampāti, the mighty Hanumān leapt across the salt ocean, a hundred yojanas wide.
t.1.1.58: There, having reached Laṅkā, the city guarded by Rāvaṇa, he saw Sītā, lost in thought, dwelling in the Aśoka grove.
t.1.1.59: Having presented the token of recognition and having delivered the news, and having consoled Vaidehī, he smashed the archway.
t.1.1.60: Having slain five commanders of the army and seven sons of ministers as well, and having crushed the valiant Akṣa, he then submitted to capture.
t.1.1.62: Then, having burned the city of Laṅkā, all except Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, the great monkey came back again to tell Rāma the pleasing news.
t.1.1.61: Knowing that by the Grandfather's boon he would be freed from the weapon, the hero, of his own free will, put up with those rākṣasas who had bound him.
t.1.1.63: He of immeasurable spirit, approaching the great-souled Rāma and circumambulating him, reported truthfully, "Sītā has been seen."
t.1.1.64: Then, accompanied by Sugrīva, he went to the shore of the great ocean and agitated the sea with arrows resembling the sun.
t.1.1.65: And the Ocean, lord of rivers, revealed himself, and at the Ocean's word he had Nala build a bridge.
t.1.1.67: By that great deed of the great-souled Rāghava, the three worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings, together with the hosts of gods and seers, were gladdened.
t.1.1.66: Crossing by that bridge to the city of Laṅkā and slaying Rāvaṇa in battle, he consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā as lord of the rākṣasas.
t.1.1.68: Thus honored by all the deities, who were supremely pleased, Rāma, having accomplished what was to be done, then rejoiced, freed from his distress.
t.1.1.70: At Nandigrāma, having cast off his matted locks, the sinless Rāma, together with his brothers, having regained Sītā, obtained the kingdom once again.
t.1.1.69: Having obtained boons from the deities and having raised the monkeys back to life, he then mounted that Puṣpaka and went to Nandigrāma.
t.1.1.72: Nowhere will any men ever see the death of a son, and women, devoted to their husbands, will always remain unwidowed.
t.1.1.71: The people are thrilled and joyful, contented and well-nourished, thoroughly righteous, free from affliction and disease, and untouched by the fear of famine.
t.1.1.73: There is no fear whatsoever arising from wind, creatures do not drown in the waters, and there is no fear whatsoever arising from fire; it is just as it was in the Kṛta age.
t.1.1.75: Rāghava will establish royal dynasties a hundredfold, and in this world he will appoint the four varṇas each to its own dharma.
t.1.1.74: Having performed hundreds of horse sacrifices, and likewise sacrifices rich in gold, and having given a hundred billion cows to the learned according to the prescribed rites,
t.1.1.76: Having ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years and ten hundred years, Rāma will go to the world of Brahmā.
t.1.1.77: This account of Rāma's deeds is purifying, destructive of sin, meritorious, and equal to the Vedas. Whoever reads it is freed from all sins.
t.1.1.78: The man who reads this Rāmāyaṇa, a tale that bestows long life, is honored in heaven after death, together with his sons and grandsons and all his kin.
t.1.1.79: A twice-born who recites it would attain eminence in speech; a kṣatriya would attain lordship over the earth; a merchant would attain profit from his wares; and even a śūdra would attain greatness.
